# Introduction

This book teaches empirical replication through short, self-contained exercises. Each one asks you to rebuild a published paper's results, then write up what replicated, what didn't, and why. Undergraduate econometrics is recommended but not required.

Before the first exercise, get your tools set up. Do this once, carefully, and every exercise after this one starts from the same foundation.

## Install R and RStudio

R and RStudio are two different pieces of software. R is the actual programming language; RStudio is an interface that makes R easier to work with. Install them in that order.

1.  Install R from [cran.r-project.org](https://cran.r-project.org). Choose your operating system and take the latest release.
2.  Install RStudio Desktop (free) from [posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop](https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop). RStudio will find your R installation automatically.

Open RStudio, not R directly, for everything in this book.

## Create a GitHub Account

Git is a program that helps keep track of your code changes. It's a bit like "track changes" in microsoft word, but much more useful. GitHub hosts this on the cloud so that you can recover your work if you accidentally delete something, your machine dies, or if you want your partner to get the most recent version.

Honestly, Git and GitHub are **not** easy to wrap your head around. But, once you get it set up and you get in the habit of 'commits' and 'pushes' you'll find it useful. I

1.  Sign up at [github.com](https://github.com).
2.  Turn on two-factor authentication (Settings → Password and authentication).
3.  GitHub no longer accepts your account password for pushing code from your computer. You'll need a personal access token instead — Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens → Generate new token (classic) works fine for this course. Save it somewhere you can find it; you'll be asked for it the first time you push from a new machine, in place of a password.

## Set Up a Folder Structure

Any scientific inquiry should address four questions:

1.  Why did we do this?

2.  How did we do this?

3.  What did we find?

4.  What does it mean?

This means that, very generally, scientific output (papers, presentations) also has four parts, though there maybe extra divisions if the answers are lengthy.

1.  Introduction

2.  Methodology

3.  Results

4.  Conclusion

Generally, you won't use much code for the Introduction or Conclusion. So, we'll focus on parts 2 and 3.

In economics, the Methodology sections are often split into two parts: Data and Econometric Approach. Unless your data set requires absolutely no changes (so never) your file structure will be something like

- Data

  - Original Data (what you downloaded, pristine)

  - Saved Data (what you have imported, cleaned, merged, etc.)

  - Dictionaries (not required but very useful for large data set)

- Scripts

  - Data Processing (the scripts that import, clean, merge, etc.)

  - Descriptive (the data visualization scripts)

  - Analysis (the scripts that implement the econometric approach)

  - R (the re-usable functions that are not specific to this project)

- Results

  - Figures

  - Tables

Consistency across exercises will save you time later. This book uses the same structure for every exercise:

```         
your-exercise/
  data/
    original data/     raw files exactly as downloaded, never edited by hand
    saved data/        cleaned data your scripts produce
  scripts/ 
    Run All           this script uses "source" to run everything
    data processing/  these scripts will import, merge, and clean data
    analysis/         these scripts will generate figures and tables (what you will put in "Results")
    descriptives/     these scripts will make 
  R/
  results/                 
    figures/            analysis scripts will save figures to here
    tables/             
  README.md              what this project is and how to run it
```

Some core ideas/tricks

1.  Keep each different set of data in a different folder in *original data*, this will make it easier to describe when you write your **Data** section

2.  *original data* is read-only. If a script needs to change something about the data, it reads from `original data/`, transforms it, and writes the result to `saved data/` — it never edits the original file in place. That way you can always regenerate everything from scratch and trust that the raw data hasn't quietly drifted from what you originally downloaded

3.  Scripts correspond to what you are going to write. Keep your scripts short and simple and writing will be short and simple.

4.  If you use a piece of code more than twice, make it a function, put it in the R folder and call it with `source()` as needed

## Create a Project

In RStudio: **File → New Project → New Directory → New Project**. Name it and choose where to save it — this should be the folder structure you just planned.

Creating a project adds a `.Rproj` file to that folder. This does two things worth understanding: it fixes your working directory to that folder (so file paths in your scripts can be relative, like `"data/original data/file.csv"`, instead of a full path that only works on your computer), and it keeps RStudio settings specific to that project. Always open your work by double-clicking the `.Rproj` file, not by opening a random `.R` script — that's what keeps the relative paths working.

## Link the Project to a GitHub Repository

There are two ways to connect a project to GitHub; either works.

**Starting on GitHub:** Create a new repository on github.com first (choose whether it's public or private). Then in RStudio, **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**, and paste the repository's URL. RStudio clones it and sets up the project for you, already connected.

**Starting in RStudio:** If you already created the project as described above, check the "Create a git repository" box when you set it up (or turn it on later via **Tools → Project Options → Git/SVN**). This starts version tracking locally, but doesn't connect to GitHub yet — for that, create an empty repository on github.com, then from a terminal inside your project run:

``` bash
git remote add origin https://github.com/YOUR-USERNAME/YOUR-REPO.git
git push -u origin main
```

Either way, once it's connected, RStudio's **Git** tab (top right pane) is where you'll do most of your version control: check boxes next to changed files, write a commit message, click **Commit**, then **Push** to send it to GitHub.
